questions.stem: A 70-year-old has a calcified, stenotic aortic valve. Serum calcium and phosphate are normal. Which process explains the calcification?
questions.explanation: Calcium deposits in damaged tissue with normal serum calcium: dystrophic. B: Metastatic calcification requires hypercalcemia and affects normal tissue. C: Hemosiderin is iron. D: Lipofuscin is wear-and-tear pigment. E: Steatosis is fat.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 30–32

questions.stem: A liver biopsy shows coarse golden-brown granules in hepatocytes that stain blue with Perls stain. Which pigment is it?
questions.explanation: Iron-containing hemosiderin is Prussian/Perls blue positive (e.g., hemochromatosis). A: Lipofuscin is Perls negative. B: Bilirubin is yellow-green and Perls negative. C: Melanin is Perls negative. E: Carbon is black (anthracosis).
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slide 28

questions.stem: A kidney section shows a wedge-shaped pale area where tubular and glomerular outlines are preserved but nuclei are absent, with inflammatory cells at the edge. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Preserved architecture without nuclei = coagulative necrosis from ischemia. A: An abscess destroys architecture. B: Caseous necrosis has granulomas. D: Fat necrosis affects adipose tissue. E: Fibrinoid necrosis is in vessel walls.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 4–5, 11

questions.stem: A lung lymph node from a city dweller has macrophages packed with black pigment. The patient has no respiratory symptoms. What is this?
questions.explanation: Inhaled carbon (exogenous pigment) in macrophages is anthracosis, usually harmless. A: Hemosiderin is golden-brown. B: Melanin is endogenous, mainly in skin. C: Lipofuscin is yellow-brown and intracellular. D: Caseous necrosis is a granulomatous necrosis.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 24–25

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with multiple myeloma has a serum calcium of 14 mg/dL. Calcium deposits are found in previously normal kidneys, lungs, and gastric mucosa. Which process is this?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia causes calcium deposition in normal tissues: metastatic calcification. A: Dystrophic calcification occurs in injured or dead tissue with normal calcium metabolism. C: Psammoma bodies are a form of dystrophic calcification in some tumors (outside slides). D: Saponification is calcium binding fatty acids in necrotic fat, not driven by hypercalcemia. E: Hemosiderin is an iron pigment, not calcium.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slide 30

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease has a black, dry, shriveled toe. Over several days it becomes swollen, moist, and foul-smelling. What best explains the change?

options.B: Trauma caused fat necrosis of the toe

questions.explanation: Dry gangrene is coagulative necrosis of an ischemic limb; superimposed bacterial infection adds liquefactive action of bacteria and leukocytes = wet gangrene. A: Caseous necrosis is seen in TB granulomas. B: Fat necrosis occurs in pancreatitis and breast. D: Fibrinoid necrosis is a vessel-wall pattern. E: Calcification wouldn't make the toe moist and foul-smelling.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 21–22

questions.stem: At autopsy, the heart of an 88-year-old is small and brown. Myocytes contain fine brownish-yellow granules that are negative on Perls stain. What is the pigment?
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is the brownish-yellow wear-and-tear pigment of aging and atrophy (heart, liver, brain). A: Hemosiderin is Perls/Prussian blue positive. B: Melanin is made by epidermal melanocytes. C: Bilirubin gives a diffuse yellow color (jaundice). D: Carbon is black (anthracosis).
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 28, 35
